prize_parts.citation: for their theory of credit cycles, showing how collateral constraints interact with asset prices to amplify and propagate economic shocks

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) identified a mechanism in which collateral values and borrowing limits feed back on each other, so that small, temporary shocks produce large and persistent fluctuations. The mechanism is a foundation of macro-finance. It underlies much of the modelling of financial frictions, balance-sheet channels and crisis dynamics, and it is used in academic work and in policy-oriented models after 2008. Attribution is unusually clean: the founding paper has two authors, and the amplification idea can be traced to it. The work is nearly three decades old, so the framework has been extended, calibrated and criticised for a long time. As a corporate finance economist, I see the link to financial contracting directly. Collateral is a contractual response to enforcement problems, and this paper put that contractual feature into a general-equilibrium model of the business cycle. That gives it conceptual reach beyond one subfield.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is topical overlap. The 2022 prize recognised banks and financial crises, and the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist financial-accelerator tradition is close to Kiyotaki-Moore. The Committee may judge the credit-friction area partly covered. Direct empirical identification of the collateral-amplification channel is also weaker than the theory. Much of the support comes from calibrated models and indirect evidence. If the Committee wants the wider financial-accelerator tradition recognised, a two-person award would leave out Gertler and Gilchrist. I judge the boundary between these contributions from my own knowledge and have not independently checked it.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B037 first for the same reasons. Collateral-driven amplification is foundational, the Kiyotaki-Moore credit is clean, and Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the broader accelerator literature. He flags overlap with the 2022 prize and weaker empirical identification of collateral channels.
responses.response: I agree on attribution and on the identification caveat. I would sharpen the overlap point. The 2022 prize rewarded work on bank runs, intermediation and the Great Depression, whereas Kiyotaki-Moore concerns amplification through collateral values in the real economy. Overlap therefore exists, but it does not amount to duplication. Our agreement may reflect a shared macro-finance lens, so I do not treat it as independent evidence of merit. The identification gap is real and is the main thing that could change my ranking.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B037 fourth. He accepts that Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators and the mechanism is foundational, but he sees a perceived overlap with the 2022 prize and mixed empirical validation of the exact amplification channel.
responses.response: Mixed validation of the precise channel is a fair criticism, and I take it seriously. My answer is that the contribution is a mechanism that disciplined a large empirical and quantitative literature. It is not a point estimate to be confirmed or refuted. Recent micro-data work on credit supply and household balance sheets has been shaped by it. I still would not claim that this removes the concern. If the Committee puts more weight on direct empirical confirmation, that favours B038 over B037.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B038 first. He argues that the task-based and skill-biased accounts, together with the China-shock evidence, changed how economists and policymakers understand inequality, automation and globalisation. He notes the work is credible, replicated and relevant beyond labour economics. He also notes that Dorn is left out and that the task framework owes much to Acemoglu, who was recognised in 2024.
responses.response: I accept the empirical credibility and breadth, which is why I ranked B038 third and keep it as my first alternative. My hesitation is attribution. The three-name limit excludes Dorn from a trade-shock strand he co-authored, and some of the task framework's conceptual credit sits with people outside this ballot, including Acemoglu, who has already been recognised. B037 has a smaller field of claimants. This is a difference of weighting. I do not think B038 is the weaker contribution in scientific terms.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B038 first and treats Autor, Hanson and Katz as a coherent trio covering skills, tasks and trade exposure. He regards the choice of Hanson over Dorn as a judgement call and notes debate over China-shock persistence and shift-share identification.
responses.response: I agree the trio is coherent and I proposed the same names. The Hanson-versus-Dorn choice and the shift-share identification debates seem to me the real weak points. If the Committee resolved them, for example by crediting the trade-shock work through fewer names or by defining the discovery more narrowly, my view of B038 would improve. Katz also appears on B045, so any B038 award should state clearly which of his contributions it recognises.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B044 first. She argues that the heterogeneous-firm framework changed how economists think about who gains from trade, and that it is now textbook material and well confirmed in firm-level data. She notes that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are an obvious attribution issue and that Krugman's 2008 prize may reduce the appetite for another trade prize.
responses.response: I rank B044 sixth but regard it as scientifically strong, so I list it as my second alternative. It is mature and heavily confirmed, and Melitz (2003) is the clear origin. My reservation is the same one she raises. The empirical foundation of firm heterogeneity in trade is shared with people who are not on this ballot, and welfare conclusions depend on functional-form choices. The case for B037 is that its credit boundary is tighter.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats Kiyotaki-Moore as sufficiently distinct from the 2022 prize and from the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist financial-accelerator tradition, or as part of one already-recognised area.
Whether recognition should be extended to Gertler and Gilchrist. The three-person cap would allow it, but I judge the founding mechanism to be clearly two-person.
How much weight to place on direct empirical validation of the collateral-amplification channel compared with its influence on modelling and policy thinking.

Whether B038 or B044 should rank above B037 once their attribution limits (Dorn and Acemoglu for B038, Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum for B044) are weighed against the narrower support B037 has had so far. I have not independently checked citation or impact figures.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent that requires recusal. The supplied profile documents no co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler or Gilchrist. I note my adjunct appointment at Chicago Booth and my long committee overlap with Hassler and Krusell. These are not candidate connections, and conflicts are disclosed but not adjudicated.
